metadata.label_rationale: Demonstrates Spring Framework Java deserialization RCE (CVE-2016-1000027) via gadget chain exploitation when untrusted data is deserialized, enabling remote code execution through classes available on the classpath (Commons Collections, ROME, etc.).

context.impact: Applications deserializing untrusted data (from caches, message queues, session stores, API responses) are vulnerable to remote code execution via gadget chain exploitation. Affected enterprises reported $12.3M in incident response costs. Issue present since Spring 4.1.4, affecting all versions through 5.3.16.
context.attack_vector: Attacker crafts serialized Java object (gadget chain) using ysoserial tool that exploits classes on target classpath (Commons Collections, ROME, Spring framework classes). When deserialized via ObjectInputStream.readObject(), gadget chain executes arbitrary code through method chaining across trusted libraries. No authentication required if serialized data accepted from untrusted sources.

conversations.value: My Spring Boot application caches user objects in Redis for performance. I serialize the objects using standard Java ObjectOutputStream. Is there any security risk with this approach?
This is terrifying. What's the immediate fix? Do I need to rewrite my entire caching layer?

exploit_scenario.description: Application caches user objects in Redis using Java ObjectInputStream. Attacker compromises Redis or intercepts network traffic. Attacker uses ysoserial to generate serialized gadget chain object (e.g., CommonsCollections5 chain). Attacker writes malicious payload to Redis cache: SET user:victim_id (malicious serialized bytes). When application calls getCachedUser() and executes ois.readObject(), gadget chain instantiates. During object reconstruction, method chaining across CommonsCollections library executes attacker's embedded command. Example chain: ChainedTransformer -> InvokerTransformer -> Runtime.getRuntime().exec(attacker_command). Result: Arbitrary command execution on application server. Attacker gains shell, reads database credentials, pivots to internal systems.
preconditions: Spring Framework 4.1.4 through 5.3.16 (or any version using ObjectInputStream)
Application deserializes untrusted data from Redis, database, file, or network
Gadget chain library present on classpath (Commons Collections < 3.2.2, ROME, Spring classes, etc.)
No ObjectInputFilter or input validation on deserialized classes
Attacker can write to Redis cache or intercept serialized data

secure_properties: JSON serialization used exclusively (Jackson, Gson, etc.) instead of Java ObjectInputStream
ObjectInputFilter configured with strict whitelist if Java deserialization unavoidable
Gadget chain libraries upgraded to patched versions (Commons Collections 3.2.2+, 4.0+)
All transitive dependencies scanned and vulnerable versions excluded
Runtime monitoring detects suspicious deserialization patterns
SAST rules block ObjectInputStream usage in code review
No Commons Collections < 3.2.2 or unpatched ROME libraries on classpath
ObjectInputStream.setObjectInputFilter() called before readObject() if legacy code
Classes allowed in ObjectInputFilter limited to specific application classes only
negative_properties: Must NOT use ObjectInputStream for untrusted data deserialization
Must NOT rely on Application.readObject() security without ObjectInputFilter
Must NOT include Commons Collections < 3.2.2 in pom.xml directly or transitively
Must NOT deserialize objects from user input, APIs, or caches without filtering
Must NOT assume Java serialization is safe—gadget chains don't require custom code
Must NOT mix trusted and untrusted data in same serialization stream
Must NOT skip dependency scanning for gadget chain libraries
